citation.sourceDocument: KFF, Status of State Medicaid Expansion Decisions (2026-08-21); 42 U.S.C. §1396a(a)(10)(A)(i)(VIII) and (e)(14)(I)
citation.sourceNote: The ACA's Medicaid expansion covers adults up to 138% of the federal poverty level — nominally 133% plus a 5-percentage-point income disregard, which is why both numbers appear in the literature for the same rule. NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) made expansion optional for states, so whether a household qualifies depends first on which state it is in; this shard is that map. The District of Columbia used to carry its own override here, 215% (210% plus the 5-point disregard), and no longer does: DHCF's Medicaid Director Letter MDL 25-02 (October 16, 2025) lowered the limit for childless adults and parents and caretaker relatives to 138% effective January 1, 2026, under the FY2026 Budget Support Act (Bill 26-260), and moved adults from 138% to 200% to the Healthy DC Plan, which is not Medicaid. The shard kept 215% until 2026-10-19, telling a DC adult between the two lines that they qualified. The CMS eligibility-levels table this audit reads still shows DC at 210% because it predates the change. What it does NOT decide is eligibility. Non-expansion states still cover children, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and very-low-income parents under separate pathways with their own thresholds, and several of them leave a COVERAGE GAP: adults over the parent limit but under 100% of poverty, who earn too much for Medicaid and too little for a marketplace subsidy. The shard also does not carry asset tests, immigration-status rules, the MAGI household-composition rules (which differ from a tax household), medically needy spend-down, or the state-by-state variation in what Medicaid covers once you have it. Treat the answer as "is expansion available where you live, and does your income fall under it" — a first question, not a determination. A state can also change its position by ballot measure or legislation — and thirteen of the forty-one that expanded have a TRIGGER LAW that would end or curtail expansion coverage automatically if the enhanced federal matching rate drops, with no new vote required: AR, AZ, IA, ID, IL, IN, MT, NC, NH, NM, OH, UT, VA.
